title: PC prices to remain elevated until end of 2027
summary: IDC has bad news for enterprises upgrading PCs: don’t expect prices to come down any time soon. PC prices are already high due to constrained supplies and surging memory and component costs. Geopolitical tensions and an uncertain global economy won’t make the situation any better. “A weaker economy could soften demand further, and with prices still high and supply constrained, the outlook for the remainder of 2026 and going into 2027 could deteriorate,” IDC analysts said in a press release last week. The third quarter of 2026 was a disaster for PC makers, with shipments falling 20.1% year over year. PC makers and their channel partners stocked up on inventory earlier in the year ahead of memory-driven price hikes. The focus in the third quarter was on clearing out that leftover inventory amid dried-up demand. “Channels are now worried about carrying too much inventory into a market where high prices are suppressing demand,” said Jitesh Ubrani, a research director at IDC. Within the existing inventory, low-cost PCs are harder to find. For example, HP is making higher-priced PCs a larger part of its product mix so it can generate higher revenue amid declining PC shipments. HP’s chief financial officer, Karen Parkhill, said in an August earnings call that the company is prioritizing “higher-value unit placements, repricing for higher commodity costs” to offset the lower volume of PC shipments. “We continue to expect memory and storage costs to increase further as a percentage of the bill of materials,” Parkhill said. Enterprises picked up new PCs earlier in anticipation of price increases and are now pulling back, said analyst Jack Gold of J. Gold Associates. That’s partially because PC makers are passing higher memory and component costs on to customers, Gold said. Many new PCs have AI hardware accelerators and qualify as AI PCs . title: 16 advanced Android messaging features you’ve probably never noticed
summary: Messaging on Android has come an impressively long way in a relatively short time. After years of comically extreme flipping and flopping and endless-seeming strategy shifts , Google’s been focused on its Google Messages Android app as the primary platform for Android messaging for a solid several years now. And that almost shockingly unusual ( for Google! ) dedication is starting to make a noticeable difference. At this point, here in the frequently overwhelming year of 2026, messaging on Android is actually a pretty decent experience. The Google Messages app is solid at its core — and, all basics aside, the service is packed with easily overlooked efficiency enhancers and experience-improving options. As a follow-up to my collection of 12 time-saving Android texting tricks , I wanted to dive even deeper and explore some of Google Messages’ other oft-overlooked advantages — advanced features that are all too easy to miss but that can make your Android messaging adventures even more productive and pleasurable. title: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong | Richard Hermer
summary: Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future In my two years as attorney general, I spent more time working on national security than any other issue. The range and gravity of the threats posed to our nation are multifold, from terrorism, armed conflicts and nuclear proliferation, to the impacts of financial insecurity and the climate crisis. All profound challenges, yet ones our superb intelligence and defence communities are well placed to counter. The risk from AI is of an altogether different magnitude, not only in scale, but also because there is a limited time window to address it. The risk is difficult to overestimate: it poses an existential risk to humanity. The lights are flashing red and we must act now before it’s too late. Although the extraordinary threats posed by AI have long been flagged by those closely involved in its creation, it was not until very recently, after the disclosure of the Hugging Face hack and the resignation of Jacob Coxon from Anthropic , that the issue at last started to gain traction in the public discourse. This moment is an opportunity, and to capitalise on it we desperately need increased urgency in international coordination to regulate frontier AI. There must also be meaningful public engagement with how AI should be shaped to benefit humanity, rather than entrench the power of a few. We cannot leave this to China, the US and big tech – we must all demand a voice in the debate. Continue reading...

title: Hands-on agentic development with Google’s Antigravity IDE
summary: Google Antigravity IDE is one of the most sophisticated integrated development environments available today. In contrast to Antigravity 2.0 , which focuses exclusively on managing agents, or Antigravity CLI , which is a way to interact with agents from the command line, Antigravity IDE covers the spectrum from a basic code editor, to an auto-completion engine, to an AI-powered editor, to a full-blown multi-agent orchestrator. Antigravity IDE uses Google’s Gemini models, and optionally Claude models. And it boasts several state-of-the-art features for agentic software development: Multi-agent: Antigravity IDE can spawn and orchestrate multiple agents working in parallel. Planning: Antigravity IDE will generate task lists and detailed implementation plans for approval and modification. Project awareness: Antigravity IDE understands your project’s structure and can run terminal commands and respond to their output. Interactivity: Antigravity IDE can run web searches and open a Chrome browser window to test a web app via the UI. One of the most important factors in modern AI-driven development is the divide between programmers and non-programmers. There is a sense that the “citizen developer” or non-technical user has been empowered to build software. And to some extent, that is true. But the reality is that the AI only gets you so far before demanding some expertise. Antigravity IDE is clean enough to be inviting to the non-developer. However, its most compelling features, the multi-agent orchestration and detailed implementation planning, will quickly call for knowledge of the architecture and internals of the application or system you intend to build. Even the clearest of natural language will become impenetrable jargon if you don’t have some grounding in concepts like dependencies, server routes, and database schemas. title: Why data work is one step behind on AI
summary: One of the reasons programmers “got” agentic AI first, in the sense that it could meaningfully alter their productivity and effectiveness, is because code could be checked. They turn agents loose on a function, read the diff, run the tests, and decide whether to keep it. Output comes back to them in a form they already know how to read, so trusting the machine didn’t necessarily require a ton of faith. The folks who work with data all day long sit one step back from the same door. People in business and financial operations roles outnumber software developers in the US by about six to one , and they’ve thus far picked up a small fraction, at best, of the productivity gain that engineering has absorbed. Yes, they can describe the analysis they want, which is what requires their specialized knowledge. What comes back to them is a number or a chart, or maybe two hundred lines of code, none of which shows an analyst how the results were produced. The output, in other words, cannot automatically be assumed to have used the right pieces of data, combined it correctly, and finally computed with the right formulas. Or maybe the agent missed a bunch of the data. The result is a black box, which isn’t something that should breed confidence. The question then becomes why , and there are three solvable variables. Problem 1. The user’s own data is out of reach A business user’s data sits in spreadsheets, files in SharePoint, applications such as Salesforce, and data platforms such as Databricks, Snowflake, or BigQuery. Getting to it means filing a request with a data platform team whose responsibility is governing everything. Of course, as just about any data platform engineer will tell you, the team’s headcount is undersized for the requests it receives, and what the business user gets as a workaround is often a copy of a copy. Maybe it’s a CSV that was pulled a couple of months ago, or a workbook that has been handed off four times with untracked changes. Then when an agent go

title: Is your software product ready for the Cyber Resilience Act?
summary: The European Union is rolling out new cybersecurity requirements for hardware and software products sold in the EU market. Aimed at ensuring that all products “with digital elements” are safe from cyber threats, the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) has implications for the manufacturers of everything from smartwatches and smartphones to data center and industrial equipment — and for the producers of all the software that runs on these devices. The CRA applies to all products that include a digital component that are made available for sale to customers in the region, whether those products are made by the companies themselves or are part of a bigger distribution chain. Among other requirements, the CRA forces any manufacturer to design their products so that they can be updated if and when a security issue is discovered. Many developers outside the EU are not familiar with this regulation. Yet not understanding what it covers could lead to sales being blocked or to potential fines. The deadline is also closer than you might think — while the full Act comes into force in December 2027, the first reporting requirements began in September 2026. Products must meet 13 guidelines Under the CRA, all products with a software component will have to meet 13 guidelines. These cover a range of requirements on how they handle any data that is created during use, how that data is kept private, and security for the software itself. The product itself should be resilient and with a limited attack service. This includes standard best practices like ensuring that the default configuration for any product is secure, that unauthorized access is not possible, and that data is held securely. Most importantly, the software implemented on any device should be capable of being updated to a more secure version. The rules also cover the data itself and how it can be managed over time. title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
summary: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . title: Is there still value in learning DE fundamentals from books and courses now that AI writes most of the code?
summary: I’ve programmed casually for about 10 years in a variety of languages, but I’ve only been doing it professionally (DE/AE) for around 3. I love this career. I used to enjoy the problem-solving of writing code myself, but what I really love is building: smart pipelines, better ways to collect metadata, simple apps that let the business interact with its data. So naturally, AI has me feeling a sense of dread. The most senior dev on my team (mostly an app developer, 20+ years of experience) now believes AI can out-code him 99% of the time. He’s smart and I trust his judgment, which makes it more disappointing. He doesn’t even think we need to review code anymore, since GitHub Copilot will flag anything problematic. On the learning side, I’ve read Fundamentals of Data Engineering , I’m partway through Designing Data-Intensive Applications , and I’ve learned Kimball’s dimensional modeling through video courses. Now I’m wondering: Is it still worth continuing this kind of deep learning? Does system-level and architectural knowledge still set you apart, or is that being automated too? Should I just learn alongside AI, questioning why it makes the choices it does? What level of learning is actually worth it these days, and how are you staying ahead? submitted by /u/TheOnlinePolak [link] [comments]
